passages.t: A rash pledge, and the ant
passages.happening:
‘My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, if you have struck hands in pledge with a stranger’ (verse 1), you have been caught by your own words. So get free. ‘Go, humble yourself, and press your plea with your neighbor’ (verse 3). Do not sleep until it is done. ‘Free yourself, like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the snare of the fowler’ (verse 5).

Then the father turns to the slacker. ‘Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise’ (verse 6). The ant has no commander or overseer, yet ‘it prepares its provisions in summer; it gathers its food at harvest’ (verse 8).

“How long will you lie there, O slacker? When will you get up from your sleep?” (verse 9). ‘A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit’ (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter steps aside from the warnings about adultery to speak of money, work and speech. Wisdom reaches into business deals and sleep habits as well as into marriage and worship.

Putting up security meant guaranteeing someone else's loan. If the borrower did not pay, the guarantor had to, sometimes with his land, his goods or even his freedom. Striking hands sealed the pledge, the way signing a contract does now. The word is arav, to stand surety, and Proverbs warns against doing it rashly several times (11:15; 17:18; 22:26-27). Israel's law also guarded the poor in lending: no interest from a poor fellow Israelite, and a poor man's cloak taken as a pledge was to be returned by nightfall.

Harvester ants were a familiar sight in Israel's fields, gathering seeds and storing them underground. The ant works without anyone forcing it.

The slacker, atsel, is one of the book's stock characters, comic and sad at once. His poverty here does not come from bad luck but from a slow pile of small choices: a little sleep, a little slumber.
passages.later: The law commanded open-handed lending to the poor: ‘Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs’ (Deuteronomy 15:8). And Agur praises the ant again: ‘The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer’ (Proverbs 30:25). Paul urges the same energy: ‘Do not let your zeal subside’ (Romans 12:11).
passages.hard:
Is it always wrong to guarantee a loan for someone, and does laziness always lead to poverty?

These are proverbs, and they describe the usual pattern, not an absolute law. The warning in verses 1 to 5 is against rash pledges, especially for a stranger, which could ruin a household. Elsewhere the Bible praises generosity and lending to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7-8; Psalm 37:26). Many interpreters understand the book to be warning against guarantees you cannot afford, or that were made in haste, not forbidding all help to others.

In the same way, verses 9 to 11 describe how laziness often leads to want. That does not mean every poor person is lazy. Proverbs itself knows of poverty caused by injustice (13:23), and it commands kindness to the poor. Reading the slacker's portrait as an explanation of all poverty misreads the book, and it can harden a reader against people in real need.
passages.asks: The ant works without a boss. Ask what you put off when no one is watching, and what a little sleep, a little slumber, is costing you. And ask whether a promise you made in haste needs to be humbly put right.

passages.happening:
‘A worthless person, a wicked man, walks with a perverse mouth, winking his eyes, speaking with his feet, and pointing with his fingers’ (verses 12-13). ‘With deceit in his heart he devises evil; he continually sows discord’ (verse 14). His ruin will come suddenly (verse 15).

Then comes a list. ‘There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are detestable to Him’ (verse 16): ‘haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that run swiftly to evil, a false witness who gives false testimony, and one who stirs up discord among brothers’ (verses 17-19).
passages.hearers:
The worthless man speaks with his whole body. Winking, shuffling his feet and pointing were signals of secret mockery or plotting in a culture where gestures carried a lot of meaning.

The list of seven uses a pattern found elsewhere in Proverbs and in the prophets: six things, yes seven, building to a climax. It moves down the body: eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet. Then it ends with the false witness and the one who stirs up discord among brothers, which ties back to the troublemaker of verse 14.

Detestable is to'evah, a strong word in the law for idolatry and gross sin. It is striking what it is used for here: arrogance, lying, and setting brothers against each other, sins many people treat as small. The practical and the spiritual are not two separate areas. These are offenses against God, not only social mistakes.
passages.later: The prophet Amos uses the same counting pattern in his words against the nations: ‘For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment’ (Amos 1:3). And the false witness of verse 19 breaks the ninth commandment: ‘You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor’ (Exodus 20:16).
passages.asks: The list puts pride and stirring up division beside the shedding of blood. Ask which of the seven you are most likely to excuse in yourself. And ask whether there is any quarrel you have been feeding that you could help to end.

passages.t: A lamp, and a fire in the lap
passages.happening:
‘My son, keep your father’s commandment, and do not forsake your mother’s teaching’ (verse 20). Bind them on your heart. ‘When you walk, they will guide you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; when you awake, they will speak to you’ (verse 22). ‘For this commandment is a lamp, this teaching is a light’ (verse 23).

It will keep him from the adulteress. ‘Do not lust in your heart for her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes’ (verse 25). ‘Can a man embrace fire and his clothes not be burned? Can a man walk on hot coals without scorching his feet?’ (verses 27-28). ‘So is he who sleeps with another man’s wife; no one who touches her will go unpunished’ (verse 29).

A hungry thief can at least repay what he stole, even sevenfold (verses 30-31). But ‘He who commits adultery lacks judgment; whoever does so destroys himself’ (verse 32). Wounds and lasting disgrace follow, and a wronged husband's fury will take no payment (verses 33-35).
passages.hearers:
The words about binding the teaching on the heart and tying it around the neck echo Deuteronomy 6, where Israel is told to keep God's words with them when they sit, walk, lie down and get up. Here the teaching becomes a companion through the whole day.

The law of theft required a thief to repay double, or four or five times for livestock he had killed or sold. Sevenfold is probably not a legal figure but a way of saying full repayment, seven being a number of completeness. The contrast is the point. A thief, however guilty, can make it right. Adultery breaks something money cannot repair.

The last verses describe a wronged husband's anger as a fact of life, to show how costly adultery is. They do not commend revenge.
passages.later: The psalm says the same of God's word: ‘Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path’ (Psalm 119:105). And the law of theft is in Exodus: ‘he must repay five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep’ (Exodus 22:1).
passages.asks: The father asks whether anyone can hold fire and not be burned. Ask what fire you are tempted to think you can hold safely. And ask whether God's word is a lamp you actually carry, when you walk, when you lie down and when you wake.
